content.intro: This lesson covers Remote Docker Engine Access. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: The Docker CLI is a client that sends requests to a Docker Engine endpoint. The daemon performs operations on images, containers, networks, and volumes; access to that endpoint is highly privileged and must be protected. Learning remote docker engine access helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Engine API concepts
items.text: The daemon/API executes requests against an Engine endpoint. Access should be limited because an unrestricted daemon can usually control host-level resources.

content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for remote docker engine access. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Remote Docker Engine Access
content_blocks.code:
docker context ls
docker context show
docker info
content_blocks.expected_output: The commands list configured endpoints, show the active context, and report Engine information for that context.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Check context/endpoint before running any mutating command, especially when using remote Docker hosts.
content_blocks.safety_note: Never enable unauthenticated remote Docker API access; protect remote endpoints with supported TLS/authentication and network controls.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
